newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Central bank says depreciation fears unwarranted.
newsitem.headline: Central bank says depreciation fears unwarranted.

text.p: Taiwan central bank vice-governor Liang Cheng-chin said on Wednesday the foreign exchange market should not have "false expectations" that the Taiwan dollar would continue to depreciate in the near term.
"Today's depreciation was the result of market expectations. I hope the market will not have this sort of false expectations," Liang told reporters after the close of trading.
Liang made the comment when asked whether the central bank expected the Taiwan dollar to fall further in the near term.
The Taiwan dollar closed sharply lower against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday, pushed to its lowest level in three months by heavy U.S. dollar demand, dealers said.
The Taiwan dollar dipped to an intrasession low of T$27.620 to the U.S. dollar before rebounding slightly to end at T$27.586 against Tuesday's T$27.550 close.

Liang gave several reasons for the bank's belief that the a significant devaluation was not warranted, noting that Taiwan's domestic economy was showing signs of recovering from its slump and that the U.S. dollar had not shown such strength as to warrant pushing the Taiwan dollar lower.
Liang also pointed out that despite the recent lowering of interest rates by key state commercial banks, rates in Taiwan were not overly low in comparison to other countries.
This meant fears of investors switching their Taiwan dollar holdings to foreign exchange to avoid what might be perceived as overly low interest rates were unjustified, he said.
After weeks of all-but-dead trading, Taiwan's foreign exchange market sprang to life in dramatic form.
Turnover through dealers was a hectic US$569.5 million, the heaviest since US$606.5 million recorded on March 15 at the height of Taiwan's acute military tensions with China.

Liang comments indicated that the central bank may have shifted away from its strategy, first seen in late May, of trying to foster a devaluation that would spur exports -- the engine of Taiwan's ailing economy.

The central bank had won economists' praise in May by trying to engineer a Taiwan dollar devaluation, announcing that it was abandoning its decade-old T$27.5 defence level to reinvigorate the sagging export economy.
That sent the dollar sliding to within a few cents of T$28 in June, but recent months have seen it bounce back to precisely the old defence level.
